name: Bupropion (Wellbutrin, Zyban)
summary: Activating antidepressant that boosts energy and motivation, with less sexual side effects and weight gain than many SSRIs. Also used to help people quit smoking.
description: Bupropion is an antidepressant that tends to feel more "activating" than sedating. People often notice more energy, better focus, and less emotional numbness compared with some other antidepressants. It can also help reduce cigarette cravings and withdrawal. Downsides: it can worsen anxiety or insomnia in some people and has a dose-related seizure risk, so doses have to be spaced out and caps are strict.
patient_summary: Bupropion helps with depression and seasonal low mood, and it can make it easier to quit smoking. Many people feel more energy and fewer sexual side effects than with SSRIs. The main things to watch for are trouble sleeping, feeling more wired or anxious, and seizures at high doses or in people with risk factors.

linked_conditions.context: First-line antidepressant option in many guidelines, especially when low energy, fatigue, or SSRI sexual side effects are major issues.
XL formulations are FDA-approved to prevent fall/winter depressive episodes in people with a history of SAD.
Bupropion SR (Zyban) is FDA-approved to help people quit smoking; typically doubles quit rates vs placebo when combined with counseling.
Sometimes used off-label when ADHD co-occurs with depression or when stimulants are not a good fit.
Often added when SSRIs cause sexual side effects; may improve libido and orgasm difficulties for some people.

contraindications: Seizure disorder or history of seizures
Current or past anorexia nervosa or bulimia
Abrupt stopping of alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or seizure medicines
Use of MAOIs now or within the last 14 days
Current use of another bupropion-containing product
Known hypersensitivity to bupropion or any component

efficacy_response.comparison_data: ≈13% with placebo (roughly doubles quit rates; NNT ~8–10)
efficacy_response.patient_text: In smoking-cessation studies, about 1 in 4 people on bupropion were smoke-free at the end of treatment, compared with about 1 in 8 on placebo.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: Typical values from large Zyban smoking cessation trials

pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Extensive first-pass metabolism; effective systemic exposure via active metabolites
pharmacokinetics.onset: Some people feel small changes in 1–2 weeks; full antidepressant effects usually take 4–6 weeks
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: IR: ~2 hours; SR: ~3 hours; XL: ~5 hours
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Parent drug ~21 hours; active metabolites ~20–37 hours
pharmacokinetics.duration: Once or twice daily dosing maintains 24-hour coverage
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic via CYP2B6 to hydroxybupropion and other active metabolites; also a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Bupropion is an antidepressant that tends to be more energizing than sedating. It’s used for depression, seasonal mood problems, and to help people stop smoking.
items: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD): Low mood, low energy, loss of interest, and trouble enjoying things
Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD): Depression that reliably shows up in the darker fall/winter months
Smoking cessation (Zyban): Reduces cigarette cravings and withdrawal, often used with nicotine patches or gum
People who had sexual side effects or emotional blunting on SSRIs and want something less likely to cause that
off_label: ADHD when stimulants are not a good fit or there is comorbid depression
SSRI-related sexual dysfunction (as an add-on or switch)
Bipolar depression (always with a mood stabilizer—never as monotherapy)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone’s experience is different, but people often describe bupropion like this:

quotes: I felt less stuck on the couch and more able to start my day.
It didn’t numb me—it just made it easier to get going.
My brain fog lifted a bit and I could actually focus.
My mood didn’t flip overnight, but little things bothered me less.
It felt like someone turned down the heaviness by a few notches.
It was subtle at first, but after a month I realized I was laughing again.
Taking it in the morning helped; if I took it late, I couldn’t sleep.
It gave me energy but also made me more wired at first.
My anxiety got a bit worse before it settled down.
items.note: Because it’s activating, some people notice more jitteriness or insomnia, especially in the first 1–2 weeks.

quotes: I switched from an SSRI and my sex drive actually came back.
I didn’t gain weight like I did on my last antidepressant.
I lost a few pounds without trying, mostly because I wasn’t snacking as much.
items.note: Compared with SSRIs, bupropion is less likely to cause sexual problems and weight gain; some people lose a small amount of weight.

quotes: Cigarettes didn’t feel as ‘rewarding’ after a couple of weeks.
Cravings were still there but less intense and easier to ride out.
It gave me just enough space between the urge and the action to actually choose not to smoke.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Bupropion doesn’t work overnight, but people typically notice changes in energy and thinking before full mood improvement.
key_points: 1–2 weeks: Some people notice more energy or slightly clearer thinking.
3–4 weeks: Mood, motivation, and day-to-day functioning often start to feel better.
4–6 weeks: Full antidepressant effect for many people.
Smoking cessation: Cravings usually ease over the first 1–2 weeks; most people set their quit date in week 2.
Duration: SR tablets are taken twice daily, XL tablets once daily, to keep levels steady over 24 hours.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: For depression, bupropion works about as well as other modern antidepressants, but feels more activating and tends to have fewer sexual and weight side effects. For smoking cessation, it roughly doubles your odds of quitting compared with going cold turkey, especially when you also get counseling and support.
sections.clinical_details: In large clinical trials, bupropion SR (Zyban) plus behavioral counseling led to continuous abstinence rates of roughly 20–30% at the end of treatment, compared with about 10–15% with placebo. For depression, head-to-head trials generally show similar response and remission rates compared to SSRIs, with a different side effect profile (more activation/insomnia, fewer sexual side effects, less weight gain).

citation.authors: Multiple randomized controlled trials of bupropion SR for smoking cessation and MDD
citation.title: Bupropion for depression and tobacco dependence

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Main serious risks: suicidal thoughts (especially under 25), seizures at high doses or in at-risk people, and higher blood pressure.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants, including bupropion, can increase suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, teenagers, and young adults, especially when starting or changing the dose. Families and caregivers should watch closely for sudden changes in mood, behavior, or thinking and contact a doctor right away if they appear.
other: Seizures: Risk goes up at higher doses, in people with seizure risk factors, and if doses are taken too close together.
Eating disorders: People with a current or past history of anorexia or bulimia should NOT take bupropion due to a significantly higher seizure risk.
Alcohol: Heavy use or suddenly stopping heavy alcohol use while on bupropion can trigger seizures.
Blood pressure: Bupropion can raise blood pressure; rarely it can cause severe hypertension.
Mental health changes: Can cause agitation, anxiety, irritability, and, rarely, hallucinations or mania—especially in people with bipolar disorder or a history of psychosis.
Eye problems: Rare cases of acute angle-closure glaucoma—sudden eye pain, red eyes, and vision changes are emergencies.
patient_counseling: Tell someone you trust that you’re starting this medication and ask them to flag big changes in your mood, sleep, or behavior.
Take doses exactly as prescribed and never more than the maximum daily dose.
If you have a history of seizures, serious head injury, or eating disorders, make sure your prescriber knows—this drug may not be safe for you.
Check your blood pressure periodically, especially if you already have high blood pressure.
Avoid binge drinking and do not suddenly stop heavy alcohol use without medical supervision.
Call a doctor or go to the ER right away if you have a seizure, sudden vision changes, severe headache, or thoughts of wanting to die.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most side effects are related to it being activating—trouble sleeping, feeling wired, dry mouth, and headaches are common. The big rare one providers worry about is seizures.
plain_language_list: Trouble sleeping if taken too late in the day
Feeling more wired, anxious, or jittery at first

common.patient_note: Most people do best taking it in the morning. If you take it in the afternoon or evening, you may find your brain is too ‘on’ to fall asleep easily.
Some people feel more wired or restless, especially in the first week or if they already have high anxiety. This often calms down with time or dose adjustment.
Feels like your mouth is sticky or cottony. Sipping water, sugar-free gum, or lozenges can help.
Usually mild and temporary. If headaches are severe or persistent, let your prescriber know.
Often improves after your body adjusts. Taking it with food can help, as can fluids and fiber for constipation.
Some people lose a modest amount of weight due to decreased appetite. This can be good or bad depending on your situation.

serious: Seizures (rare but serious; risk increases at higher doses, with certain medical conditions, or with alcohol/other drugs)
Severe allergic reactions (rash, swelling of face/lips/tongue, trouble breathing)
Severe skin reactions like Stevens–Johnson syndrome (painful rash, blisters, peeling skin, sores in mouth/eyes)
Big mood or behavior changes (agitation, aggression, suicidal thoughts, hallucinations, mania)
Severe or sudden high blood pressure (very bad headache, chest pain, vision changes)
Sudden eye pain, vision changes, or red, swollen eyes (possible acute angle-closure glaucoma)

sections.heading: Important Drug & Alcohol Interactions
sections.intro: Bupropion has two big interaction themes: seizure risk and how it affects other medications’ levels via CYP2D6.

items.with: Alcohol (heavy use, binges, or suddenly stopping)
items.risk: Much higher seizure risk and more side effects.
items.action: If you drink heavily, talk to your prescriber honestly. Do not suddenly stop heavy drinking on your own while taking bupropion—this needs medical supervision.

items.with: Other bupropion products (Wellbutrin + Zyban, or multiple strengths)
items.risk: Accidental overdose and seizures due to double dosing.
items.action: You should only be on ONE bupropion product at a time. Always check your bottles—different brand names can be the same drug.

items.with: Medicines that lower seizure threshold (some antipsychotics, antidepressants, tramadol, stimulants, certain antibiotics, etc.)
items.action: Your prescriber may choose different meds or keep doses conservative and watch more closely.

items.with: MAOIs (older antidepressants like phenelzine, tranylcypromine, selegiline, etc.)
items.risk: Dangerous blood pressure spikes and other serious reactions.
items.action: Do NOT mix. There must be at least 14 days between stopping one and starting the other.

items.with: Medicines metabolized by CYP2D6 (for example some SSRIs, SNRIs, antipsychotics, beta-blockers, tamoxifen)
items.risk: Bupropion can raise their levels and side effects.
items.action: Your doctor may lower the dose of those other meds or choose alternatives. Don’t adjust on your own.

items.risk: Mild increase in blood pressure; otherwise generally safe and often helpful together.
items.action: Often used in combination for smoking cessation. Your provider may monitor your blood pressure more closely.

sections.heading: Stopping Safely
sections.text: Bupropion does not usually cause the same intense withdrawal symptoms that SSRIs or benzodiazepines can, but you still don’t want to stop suddenly if you’ve been on it for a while.
key_points: If you’ve only been on it for a couple of weeks, your doctor may stop it more quickly.
After longer-term use (months or years), most prescribers slowly lower the dose over 1–2 weeks or more.
Stopping abruptly can lead to mood dip, irritability, rebound depression, and trouble sleeping.
If your mood crashes or you feel very off while tapering, let your prescriber know—your taper may need to be slowed down.

sections.heading: Dosing Information (Adults)
sections.text: There are three main versions: IR (immediate-release, 3×/day), SR (sustained-release, 2×/day), and XL (extended-release, 1×/day). Most people today use SR or XL.

adult.mdd_ir_initial: 100 mg twice daily, at least 6 hours apart
adult.mdd_ir_max: 450 mg/day in divided doses; no single dose >150 mg
adult.mdd_sr_initial: 150 mg once daily in the morning for 3 days
adult.mdd_sr_target: 150 mg twice daily (300 mg/day total), at least 8 hours apart
adult.mdd_xl_initial: 150 mg once daily in the morning
adult.mdd_xl_target: 300 mg once daily after several days if tolerated
adult.mdd_xl_max: 450 mg once daily (Forfivo XL 450 mg tablet)
adult.sad_xl: Start 150 mg each morning in early fall; increase to 300 mg after 1 week if tolerated; taper off in spring.
adult.smoking_sr: 150 mg once daily for 3 days, then 150 mg twice daily; usually continued for at least 7–12 weeks. Most people set their quit date in week 2.
adult.elderly: Often start lower (eg, 100 mg/day or 150 mg every other day) and titrate slowly.
adult.hepatic_impairment: Lower doses and/or less frequent dosing; severe cirrhosis often requires major dose reduction.
adult.renal_impairment: May need dose reduction or less frequent dosing, especially with significant kidney disease.

sections.simple_explanation: To lower seizure risk, doses are capped and spread out. You should never crush XL or SR tablets or take extra doses close together.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding & Special Groups
sections.text: Decisions here are very individual and should be made with an experienced prescriber who knows your history.
sections.pregnancy: Overall, bupropion is not a ‘first pick’ if you’re starting an antidepressant while pregnant, but many people who are already stable on it stay on it through pregnancy when the risk of relapse is high. Data so far do not show a big overall rise in birth defects, but there have been mixed signals about heart defects in some studies. Untreated depression also carries real risks for both parent and baby, so the decision is about balancing risks, not chasing zero risk.
sections.lactation: Small amounts of bupropion and its metabolites appear in breast milk. Most reports show no obvious problems in nursing infants, but there have been rare reports of possible seizures and irritability. If used while breastfeeding, babies should be watched for unusual sleepiness, feeding problems, or strange movements.
sections.pediatrics: Not approved for depression or smoking cessation in children. Sometimes used off-label in teens with careful monitoring, especially if there’s comorbid ADHD and depression. Suicidality monitoring is critical.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially blood pressure changes, insomnia, and agitation. Start low, go slow, and monitor blood pressure and mood closely.
sections.seizure_risk: People with a history of seizures, serious head injuries, brain tumors, eating disorders, or heavy alcohol/benzo use are at higher risk. In many of these cases bupropion is avoided altogether.

sections.heading: What Your Clinician Will Watch
items: Mood, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts—especially in the first 1–2 months and after dose changes.
Blood pressure and heart rate, particularly if you have hypertension or are using nicotine replacement.
Sleep patterns and daytime activation (too wired, too flat, or just right).
Any signs of seizures (even brief episodes of staring, jerking, or confusion).
Interactions with other meds metabolized by CYP2D6 (for example some antidepressants, antipsychotics, and heart medications).
For smoking cessation: number of cigarettes per day, cravings, and triggers.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Same drug, different release speeds. Your prescriber will usually pick the version that best fits your schedule and side effect pattern.
items: Immediate-Release (IR) Tablets: 75 mg, 100 mg – usually taken 3 times a day; used much less often now.
Sustained-Release (SR / 12-hour): 100 mg, 150 mg, 200 mg – typically 2 times a day; Zyban 150 mg SR is the smoking-cessation version.
Extended-Release (XL / 24-hour): 150 mg, 300 mg, 450 mg – taken once each morning.
Hydrobromide XL (Aplenzin): 174 mg, 348 mg, 522 mg – equivalent to 150 mg, 300 mg, 450 mg of the hydrochloride salt.

sections.heading: How It Works in the Brain
sections.text: Bupropion mainly boosts two brain chemicals: dopamine and norepinephrine. These are involved in motivation, reward, focus, and energy. Unlike SSRIs, it doesn’t strongly affect serotonin and usually doesn’t cause emotional ‘numbing’ or sexual side effects to the same degree. It also blocks certain nicotine receptors, which makes cigarettes feel less satisfying and eases withdrawal when quitting.

sections.heading: Where It Fits in Treatment
sections.text: Bupropion is often chosen when someone is depressed but also tired, low-energy, struggling with focus, or frustrated by sexual side effects or weight gain from SSRIs. It’s also a go-to option for people who want one medication that can help with both depression and smoking. It’s usually not the best fit for people with uncontrolled anxiety, panic, severe insomnia, or a history of seizures or eating disorders.

seo.title: Bupropion (Wellbutrin, Zyban): Uses, Side Effects, Dosing & Smoking Cessation
seo.description: Bupropion (Wellbutrin, Zyban) for depression, seasonal affective disorder, and quitting smoking. How it works, how long it takes, seizure risk, side effects (anxiety, insomnia, weight, sex), and who it’s best for.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and aligned with current FDA labeling and major practice guidelines for depression and smoking cessation.

faqs.a: Bupropion is used to treat major depression, prevent seasonal depression (SAD), and help people quit smoking (Zyban). Doctors also sometimes use it off-label for ADHD or to offset sexual side effects from SSRIs.

faqs.q: How long does bupropion take to work?
faqs.a: Some people notice more energy or clearer thinking within 1–2 weeks, but full mood effects usually take 4–6 weeks. For quitting smoking, it’s usually started 1 week before your quit date so it’s working when you stop.

Weight gain is less common with bupropion than with many SSRIs. Some people actually lose a small amount of weight because their appetite drops. That said, everybody’s body is different, so your experience may not match the average.

Compared with SSRIs, bupropion has a much lower chance of causing sexual side effects, and it sometimes improves libido or orgasm for people who had problems on other antidepressants. It’s often chosen for that reason.

Because it’s activating, some people feel more wired, jittery, or anxious at first—especially if they start at a higher dose or already have strong anxiety. This often gets better with time, morning dosing, or a slower titration. For people whose main problem is severe anxiety or panic, other meds are usually tried first.

faqs.q: How does bupropion help you quit smoking?
faqs.a: It works on brain chemicals linked to reward and on nicotine receptors. Cigarettes usually feel less satisfying, cravings are less intense, and withdrawal symptoms are easier to manage. It works best when combined with coaching or counseling and sometimes nicotine patches or gum.

faqs.q: Can I take bupropion with an SSRI?
faqs.a: Yes, that’s common. Many people stay on an SSRI for mood and add bupropion to help with energy, focus, and sexual side effects. Because bupropion affects how some drugs are broken down, your prescriber may adjust your SSRI dose and watch for side effects.

faqs.q: How high is the seizure risk?
faqs.a: For people without risk factors and staying within max doses, the seizure risk is low (well under 1%). The risk rises if you go over the dose limits, have a seizure history, have an eating disorder, drink heavily, or take other seizure-threshold–lowering meds. That’s why dosing rules are strict and honest history is important.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol on bupropion?
faqs.a: Light drinking may be okay for some people, but heavy drinking or binge drinking is dangerous with bupropion and raises the seizure risk. Suddenly stopping heavy alcohol use while taking bupropion is also risky. Talk realistically with your prescriber about your alcohol use before starting.

It’s not usually the first choice if you’re starting an antidepressant while pregnant, but many people who are already stable on bupropion continue it if the risk of relapse is high. Studies so far don’t show a big overall increase in birth defects, but there are some mixed data about heart defects. It’s a nuanced risk-versus-benefit conversation with your OB and mental health prescriber.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between SR and XL?
faqs.a: SR (sustained-release) is usually taken twice a day; XL (extended-release) is once a day in the morning. They contain the same active drug but release it at different speeds. Many people prefer XL for convenience and more even levels throughout the day.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss a dose?
faqs.a: If you miss a dose, just skip it and take your next dose at the normal time. Don’t double up. Taking two doses too close together can raise seizure risk.
